title: Who is my mother (Mark 3:20–35)
hook: his relatives come; he says whoever does God's will is his family; Catholics read brethren as kin, as Aramaic allows

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve, the first apostles. Your line was first, to be with him. Who did you simply spend time with? Today is day two hundred. Two hundred days of showing up. Day two hundred.

Someone in a family starts doing something the rest don't understand. Quits the job. Joins something. Moves away. And the relatives start talking. Is he all right? Has she lost it? Somebody should go and bring him home. That's where Jesus is today. The crowds are so thick he can't even eat. Mark says his own people hear about it and set out to take charge of him, because they're saying he's out of his mind. And then his mother and brothers arrive, and stand outside, and send someone in to call him. Today: who is my mother.
screen: `THE FAMILY STARTS TALKING.` → `HE'S OUT OF HIS MIND.` → `HIS MOTHER AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Mark tells this as a sandwich: family, then an argument, then family again. First, the middle. Scribes come down from Jerusalem and say Jesus drives out demons by the power of the devil. He answers with a picture: a house divided against itself cannot stand. Why would Satan fight Satan? Second, the doorway. Someone tells him: your mother and your brethren are outside, looking for you. And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who is my mother and my brethren?" He looks around at the people sitting in a circle at his feet. "Behold my mother and my brethren. For whosoever shall do the will of God, he is my brother, and my sister, and mother." It can sound cold. It isn't a rejection. It's a widening. The family is open now, to anyone who does God's will. Third, Mary. Catholics notice that no one did God's will more fully than Mary herself, who said yes to God before Jesus was born. Saint Augustine said she was more blessed for being his disciple than for being his mother. So she isn't pushed out by this saying. She's its best example. Fourth, the brethren. Who are they? Christians read this differently. Catholics believe Mary remained a virgin, and read brethren as relatives, kin, since the Bible can use brother for wider family; in Genesis, Abraham calls his nephew Lot his brother. Orthodox tradition holds they were Joseph's children from an earlier marriage. A common Protestant reading takes them as younger children of Mary and Joseph. Each reads the same verse carefully, and the text itself doesn't settle it.
screen: `A HOUSE DIVIDED CANNOT STAND.` · `BEHOLD MY MOTHER AND MY BRETHREN.` · `MARY: THE BEST EXAMPLE.` · `BRETHREN: KIN, STEP-KIN, OR SIBLINGS?` · then, large: `WHOSOEVER SHALL DO THE WILL OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a stranger as family. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you'll probably pass today without a second look: a cashier, a bus driver, a new kid at school, the neighbor you've never spoken to. Picture their face as clearly as you can. Now picture them sitting in that circle around Jesus, and hear him say: behold my brother, my sister. If you pray, hold them there for a while. If you don't, simply wish them well as you would your own family. The bell holds the time.
Brethren. The brothers at the door, whom Jesus answers by widening the family: whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, my mother. Today's word.
Your line: family by doing God's will. Today, treat one stranger the way you'd treat family: with patience, a real greeting, a little extra time. Day two hundred.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Mary as the first and most faithful disciple, and call one another brothers and sisters in Christ; the Church teaches Mary's perpetual virginity and reads the Lord's brethren as his relatives.

he widens the family to all who do God's will, and Catholics see Mary as its best example.

in Genesis, Abraham calls his nephew Lot his brother.

original.note: Greek: brothers, brethren; in Semitic usage the word behind it could cover wider kin.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus snubbed his family.
what it means: the family is widened to anyone who does God's will, with Mary as its first example.
what a scholar hears: adelphoi, read as kin (Catholic, following Jerome), step-brothers (Orthodox, following Epiphanius), or siblings (a common Protestant reading).

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 3:33–35 given from memory; confirm.
Mark 3:21: Douay has 'his friends' where others have 'his own' or 'his family'; the script says 'his own people', a paraphrase. Confirm.

Three readings of the 'brethren' given without ranking: Catholic (kin/cousins, Jerome), Orthodox (children of Joseph by an earlier marriage, Epiphanius / Protoevangelium of James), many Protestants (younger siblings). Confirm fairness.
Genesis 13:8 (Abraham to Lot, 'we are brethren') and 14:12 (Lot as his brother's son): confirm references.
Augustine's saying that Mary was more blessed in being Christ's disciple than his mother: De sancta virginitate 3 and Sermon 72A; paraphrased. Confirm.
Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (3:28–30) not discussed.
